newsitem.title: USA: Noted forecaster predicts seven Atlantic hurricanes.
newsitem.headline: Noted forecaster predicts seven Atlantic hurricanes.

text.p: The 1997 Atlantic hurricane season is likely to produce above average storm activity with seven hurricanes, capping what may turn out to be the most active three-year hurricane span on record, a noted forecaster said on Friday.
Even the recent development of an El Nino, the renowned warm water current off the west coast of South America that normally diminishes Atlantic hurricane activity, will not help.

Professor William Gray of Colorado State University, who issues hurricane forecasts four times a year, left unchanged his predictions of April when he said the current hurricane season would produce 11 tropical storms, seven of which would become hurricanes, three of them intense.

Gray noted that the El Nino, a period of warmer-than-normal water temperatures off the coast of Peru, had formed, but said it would have little impact on the formation of Atlantic hurricanes this year.
El Ninos tend to cause strong winds to blow in a westerly direction from the Pacific to the Atlantic, typically disrupting developing hurricanes.

"The many other factors we look at in the Atlantic basin are so positive for hurricane development that I do not think El Nino will play a dominant role in reducing storm activity this year," Gray said in a statement.
Gray's hurricane forecasts do not predict how many storms might make landfall or where they might hit.
Tropical depressions become tropical storms and are given names when top winds hit 39 mph (62 kph). Tropical storms become hurricanes when maximum winds reach 74 mph (118 kph).
The average Atlantic hurricane season has 9.3 tropical storms, 5.8 of which become hurricanes. Two of those hurricanes are considered intense, with sustained winds of at least 111 mph (178 kph).

Gray has been one of the most successful scientists at predicting the number and intensity of Atlantic hurricanes. He uses global weather indicators such as sea surface temperatures in the north and tropical Atlantic, rainfall in the Sahel region of West Africa where tropical systems often form, and high-level winds.

From the early 1970s to the early 1990s, the Atlantic region experienced below average hurricane activity. But 1995 produced the second largest total on record, with 19 tropical storms, 11 of which became hurricanes. Last year, there were 13 named storms, nine of which were hurricanes.

Gray said it appeared the Atlantic region was entering a period of increased hurricane activity similar to the period from the late 1940s to the late 1960s, when many major hurricanes made landfall on the east Atlantic coast, Florida and the Caribbean.
The hurricane season officially began June 1 and ends Nov. 30.
